articles.title: I'm 16 and spent a year training my own 780B language model. Here's what I learned
articles.excerpt: Hi, I'm Afonso. I'm 16, and for about the past year I've been building Ganymede, my own large language model, mostly on my own under a small lab I started called Merkium. Most write-ups about training…
articles.body: Hi, I'm Afonso. I'm 16, and for about the past year I've been building Ganymede, my own large language model, mostly on my own under a small lab I started called Merkium. Most write-ups about training LLMs come from big labs with huge teams. I wanted to share what it actually looked like from the outside, including the parts I got wrong. 1. Sparse beats dense when compute is the limit Ganymede 1.1 is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model. It has 780B parameters in total, but only about 20B are active for any given token. A router picks which experts handle each token, so you get the capacity of a very large model while paying roughly the compute cost of a much smaller one. For someone without big-lab budgets, this was the only way training and serving a model this size was realistic. 2.
articles.author: Afonso Faro

articles.title: Locking files in the browser with Web Crypto: PBKDF2, HKDF, and 1 MiB AES-GCM records
articles.excerpt: I built a small web app called Clipboard Share. Devices on the same Wi-Fi network see each other automatically, no sign-up, and you drag a file or paste some text to send it. It was made with Claude C…
articles.body: I built a small web app called Clipboard Share. Devices on the same Wi-Fi network see each other automatically, no sign-up, and you drag a file or paste some text to send it. It was made with Claude Code, and I'm the only person working on it. The thing about "same network, no account" is that anyone on that network can join the room. That's fine for a meme or a photo. It's less fine for a scan of an ID card or a contract that you want to move to a shared PC. So I added an opt-in "lock with a password" switch. This post is about how it works, with the real code, and a list of what it still doesn't do. Locking is off by default, and you turn it on per upload. What I wanted Locking is something you switch on. The normal flow gets no extra clicks.

articles.title: Why MT940 and SEPA files break, and how to check them without guessing
articles.excerpt: I'm a mechatronics engineering student in Hungary. Over the last months I wrote two small parsers/validators: one that reads bank statement files (MT940, camt.053, BAI2, CODA) and checks that the numb…
articles.body: I'm a mechatronics engineering student in Hungary. Over the last months I wrote two small parsers/validators: one that reads bank statement files (MT940, camt.053, BAI2, CODA) and checks that the numbers add up, and one that checks and converts SEPA payment files (pain.001 / pain.008). Both are deterministic: no AI, no fuzzy matching, the same file always gives the same answer. This post is about the boring part that took most of the time: the ways these "standard" files differ from the standard. If you have ever written split(":61:") and felt good about it, this is for you. Part 1: MT940 MT940 is a SWIFT text format from the 1980s.

articles.title: Check the autocomplete attribute on your signup form: a one-minute test

articles.body: A signup form that blocks autofill makes people retype their name, email and address every time. For some users that is annoying. For others it is a real barrier. It takes a minute to check. The check View the page source and look at each <input> that collects personal data. <input type= "email" name= "email" id= "email" autocomplete= "email" > <input type= "text" name= "fname" id= "fname" autocomplete= "given-name" > Look for two things: a missing autocomplete , and autocomplete="off" on fields like name and email. What the standards say The W3C's Understanding page for WCAG 1.3.5, Identify Input Purpose, says the purpose of a form input collecting information about the user must be programmatically determinable.

articles.title: BioWare Was the Greatest RPG Developer Ever
articles.excerpt: There are many great role-playing game developers, past and present. But none can touch what BioWare has done over 30-plus years.
articles.body: BioWare is dead , and my feelings are a strange cocktail of anger, sadness, and Jack’s Complete Lack of Surprise. The legendary RPG studio was bought by a private investment group earlier this year, and history shows that venture capital frequently kills what it touches, extracting whatever value out of it that it can before moving onto the next victim. It’s a hell of a contrast to the beginning of BioWare, which started out as such a pure thing. Two practicing doctors, Ray Muzyka and Greg Zeschuk, quit medicine to pursue their dream of making computer role-playing games. Sure, the studio was bought and sold a couple of times between then and now, and yes, BioWare’s recent results haven’t lived up to its venerable past, but my goodness, what a legacy this studio leaves behind.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.

articles.title: Sci-fi legend Alan Dean Foster on his new futuristic adventure 'Lost On Paradise': 'It's paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up' (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise.'
articles.body: Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, " Lost on Paradise ", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week. Foster famously ghost-wrote the first " Star Wars " novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades.
